explanations.answer: Because of the evil they had done
explanations.explanation: That's the one, baker. The LORD says the ruins are "because of the evil they have done." They provoked Him by burning incense and serving other gods (Jeremiah 44:3). The ruins have a reason, and He names it plainly.

explanations.answer: Because their walls were built too weak
explanations.explanation: Walls get blamed for a lot, friend. I once blamed my stamp for a crooked cookie when it was my own shaky hand. Nobody in this passage mentions the walls, though. The LORD points to the evil they did and the other gods they served.

explanations.answer: Because their army was far too small
explanations.explanation: I get the thinking, baker. When a city falls, you look at the soldiers first. But the army never comes up in these verses. The LORD says the ruins are "because of the evil they have done."

I can see why you'd think so, friend. But the LORD says these were gods "that neither they nor you nor your fathers ever knew." That's the opposite of old family favorites. These gods were strangers to everyone in the room.
Yes, baker. The LORD says these gods were ones "that neither they nor you nor your fathers ever knew." Nobody in the family tree had a history with them. That's a lot of incense for a stranger.

That would be a happier story, friend. But the text says they "did not listen or incline their ears." They also did not "turn from their wickedness or stop burning incense to other gods." The warnings kept coming, and the incense kept burning.

That's right, baker. The prophets warned again and again, and the people did not listen. They did not turn from their wickedness or stop burning incense to other gods (Jeremiah 44:5). Warning after warning, same smoke.

You've got it, baker. The LORD says, "Therefore My wrath and anger poured out and burned in the cities of Judah and in the streets of Jerusalem…" It's strong language, and the text means it. That's how those cities became the ruins the people could see for themselves.
I wish I could hand you that one, friend. But the verse says something heavier. It says "My wrath and anger poured out and burned." Mercy isn't the word God uses here.
That's a nice word, baker, and it's not in this verse. The LORD says, "Therefore My wrath and anger poured out and burned in the cities of Judah…" The ruins in verse 6 come from wrath, not blessing.

explanations.answer: An object of cursing and reproach
explanations.explanation: Yes, friend. The LORD says that as a result, "you will be cut off and will become an object of cursing and reproach among all the nations of the earth." That's the outcome He names for burning incense to other gods in Egypt. Nobody wants a reputation like that.

explanations.answer: Servants to the king of Egypt
explanations.explanation: That sounds like it could fit, baker. But the LORD never says anything about serving Egypt's king here. He says they will be cut off and become "an object of cursing and reproach among all the nations of the earth."

I can picture that one, friend, but it's not in the verse. The LORD talks about their name among the nations. He says they "will become an object of cursing and reproach among all the nations of the earth." No sand required.

I wish it were true, baker. But the LORD says, "To this day they have not humbled themselves or shown reverence." He adds that they have not followed His instruction or His statutes either. That's a long stretch of not bending.

That's right, friend. The LORD says, "To this day they have not humbled themselves or shown reverence…" They also haven't followed His instruction or the statutes He set before them. Humbling themselves was the one thing still not on the list.

That's the one, baker. The LORD says, "They will all fall by the sword or be consumed by famine." Then He says it again for emphasis: "From the least to the greatest, they will die by sword or famine…" No one is left off the list, from the least to the greatest.
That's dramatic, friend, but the verse doesn't say it. The LORD says the remnant will "fall by the sword or be consumed by famine." Flood and fire never show up.
I see where you're going, baker, but those two aren't in this verse. The LORD says they "will all fall by the sword or be consumed by famine." He says it twice, so it's easy to catch next time.

Yes, friend. The LORD says, "I will punish those who live in the land of Egypt, just as I punished Jerusalem, by sword and famine and plague…" Notice that plague joins the list here. The people who left Jerusalem behind were not leaving the warning behind.
I think the sound of it tricked you, baker. The LORD says, "I will punish those who live in the land of Egypt, just as I punished Jerusalem…" So Egypt is not a safe spot. The answer is True.
That's it, baker. The LORD says "none will return except a few fugitives." They long to go back to Judah, and only a few will make it. That's the sting of the verse.
That's a thoughtful guess, friend, but priests never come up in these verses. The LORD says "none will return except a few fugitives." Fugitives are the only ones He names.

I can see why you'd think that, baker. Verse 7 mentions women and children, but that was about being cut off from Judah. When it comes to who returns, the LORD says "none will return except a few fugitives."

explanations.answer: We will not listen to you
explanations.explanation: That's what they say, baker. The assembly tells Jeremiah, the prophet, "we will not listen to you!" There's no pause and no politeness. It's a flat no from a great assembly.
Oh, I wish, friend. That's what I say to my own ovens when the timer's going off. These people don't say it, though. They tell Jeremiah, the prophet, "we will not listen to you!"

explanations.answer: We will do all you say
explanations.explanation: That would have made for a very different chapter, baker. The assembly says the opposite to Jeremiah, the prophet: "we will not listen to you!" Then they go on to say what they will do instead.

explanations.answer: Plenty of food and no disaster
explanations.explanation: Yes, baker. The people say, "At that time we had plenty of food and good things, and we saw no disaster." Keep in mind that this is their own account of it. They're the ones giving the reason, and Jeremiah answers them next.
That's a nice picture, friend, but they don't say it. What they say is, "we had plenty of food and good things, and we saw no disaster." Peace with every nation isn't on their list.
I like the thought, baker, but it's not what they claim. They say, "At that time we had plenty of food and good things, and we saw no disaster." Rain never gets a mention.

That's what they say, friend. They tell Jeremiah, "from the time we stopped burning incense to the Queen of Heaven and pouring out drink offerings to her, we have lacked everything and have been perishing by sword and famine." Remember, it's their claim. Jeremiah has a different answer coming.

I think you caught the wrong end of it, baker. The people really do say it. They claim, "we have lacked everything and have been perishing by sword and famine" since they stopped. It's their own version of events, and it's what the question was asking about.
Yes, baker. Jeremiah asks, "did the LORD not remember and bring this to mind?" It's a question with an answer built right in. The incense in Judah's cities did not slip past the LORD.
That's a hopeful word, friend, but it's not Jeremiah's. He asks, "did the LORD not remember and bring this to mind?" Remembering is a different thing from forgiving, and the text says remember.
I see why you'd try it, baker. But Jeremiah asks, "did the LORD not remember and bring this to mind?" Accepting the incense is not part of his question.

I think the people's own argument got stuck in your head, friend. They said trouble started when they stopped. Jeremiah says the opposite: "Because you burned incense and sinned against the LORD and did not obey the voice of the LORD…" That's the reason he gives.

That's right, baker. Jeremiah says, "Because you burned incense and sinned against the LORD and did not obey the voice of the LORD…" The disaster is tied to the burning, not to stopping. He turns their whole argument around.

You've got it, baker. The LORD says, "I have sworn by My great name… that never again will any man of Judah living in the land of Egypt invoke My name or say, 'As surely as the Lord GOD lives.'" It's a serious oath, and He swears it by His own great name.

That's a reasonable thing to think about, friend, but the oath isn't about land. The LORD swears that never again will any man of Judah in Egypt "invoke My name or say, 'As surely as the Lord GOD lives.'"
I get why you'd pick it, baker, but houses aren't in the oath. The LORD swears that never again will any man of Judah in Egypt "invoke My name…" It's about their words, not their buildings.

That one flips the verse, friend. The LORD says, "I am watching over them for harm and not for good…" The words for good and for harm are in the opposite order from what you picked. So this answer is False.

Yes, baker. The LORD says, "I am watching over them for harm and not for good…" He then says every man of Judah in Egypt will meet his end by sword or famine. It's a heavy verse, and I think it's meant to be taken seriously.
That's the one, baker. The remnant "will know whose word will stand, Mine or theirs!" The question on the table was whose word holds up. They'll find out.
That's a fair guess, friend. But armies never enter this verse. The LORD says they "will know whose word will stand, Mine or theirs!"
I can see the pull of it, baker, since cities come up a lot in this chapter. But the verse says they "will know whose word will stand, Mine or theirs!" It's about words, not cities.

explanations.answer: He will be handed to his enemies
explanations.explanation: Yes, baker. The LORD says, "I will deliver Pharaoh Hophra king of Egypt into the hands of his enemies who seek his life…" Pharaoh Hophra is the king of the very land these people ran to. The land they picked as a hiding place has a king with trouble of his own.

explanations.answer: He will send Judah back home
explanations.explanation: That would be a kind exit, friend, but the text doesn't say it. The LORD says He will deliver Pharaoh Hophra, king of Egypt, "into the hands of his enemies who seek his life." Judah's road home is a separate matter.

That's a fun picture, baker, but it's not there. Pharaoh Hophra, king of Egypt, doesn't bow to anybody in this verse. The LORD says He will deliver him "into the hands of his enemies who seek his life."
